uncited: Regular Grid Traversal accelerates ray-scene intersection by stepping through a uniform 3D grid of cells, skipping empty space without primitive tests [S1, S2, unofficial].

It differs from hierarchical methods (e.g., [Sparse Voxel Traversal](5228-sparse-voxel-tracing.md)) by using a fixed-size array, offering high cache efficiency on GPUs for uniform data but requiring $O(N^3)$ memory [S3, unofficial].
All children use a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (3D-DDA) to traverse the grid.
The ray origin is mapped to an initial cell $(X, Y, Z)$.

Distances to the next grid boundary in each axis are tracked via $tMax$ and $tDelta$. $tDelta$ is constant per axis: $tDeltaX = dx / |dir_x|$ [S1, S2, unofficial]. $tMax$ is updated by adding $tDelta$ when the ray crosses a boundary.
The ray advances to the nearest boundary ($min(tMaxX, tMaxY, tMaxZ)$) [S1, S2, unofficial].
Regular grids are a foundational spatial acceleration structure in ray tracing [S1, S2, unofficial].
They partition space into disjoint sub-blocks, unlike BVH which partitions primitives [S2, S3, unofficial].
Effective on GPUs due to spatial locality [S3, unofficial].
